Set a random seed before each simulation question and report it. You may use standard packages unless a question asks you to write the calculation yourself. Use equal neighbor weights throughout. Here pp counts the covariates used to measure distance; do not add an intercept column to a KNN predictor matrix. R and Python use different random-number generators, so their exact simulation results need not agree.

Question 1: Estimate the bias and variance of KNN

In our previous homework, we used repeated simulations to study the behavior of linear regression estimators. We will now use the same idea for KNN. Consider the regression model

Yi=f(𝑿i)+ϵi,f(𝒙)=0.5x1+sin⁡(x2)−0.3x32, Y_i=f(\mathbf X_i)+\epsilon_i, \qquad f(\mathbf x)=0.5x_1+\sin(x_2)-0.3x_3^2,

where the three covariates are independent standard normal variables and ϵi∼𝒩(0,0.12)\epsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,0.1^2) independently of the covariates and other observations. Generate n=400n=400 training observations. Our goal is to estimate the mean response at

𝒙0=(0.5,0.7,1)𝖳. \mathbf x_0=(0.5,0.7,1)^{\mathsf T}.

Use Euclidean distance and consider k=1,3,5,…,29k=1,3,5,\ldots,29.

  1. Calculate f(𝒙0)f(\mathbf x_0). Generate one training dataset and obtain the KNN prediction at 𝒙0\mathbf x_0 for each value of kk.

  2. Independently repeat the generation of the training covariates and responses 200 times. Within each repetition, use the same training data for every value of kk. Store the predictions in a matrix with 200 rows and one column for each value of kk. Use this matrix to estimate the bias, variance, and mean squared error of the estimated mean response. Use divisor 200 when calculating the empirical variance, and verify numerically that

mean squared error=squared bias+variance. \text{mean squared error} =\text{squared bias}+\text{variance}.

Plot squared bias, variance, and mean squared error against kk in one figure. Explain the pattern and compare it with the bias-variance trade-off for ridge regression or lasso.

Answer

I wrote the KNN regression predictor myself. It computes all squared Euclidean distances from the target points to the training points, orders them, and averages the responses of the kk nearest with equal weights. The same distance ordering is reused for every kk.

Show the workflow 
f <- function(X) 0.5 * X[, 1] + sin(X[, 2]) - 0.3 * X[, 3]^2

# KNN regression with equal weights; returns one column per k
knn_reg <- function(X_train, y_train, X_new, ks) {
  X_new <- matrix(X_new, ncol = ncol(X_train))
  D <- outer(rowSums(X_new^2), rowSums(X_train^2), "+") - 2 * X_new %*% t(X_train)
  ord <- t(apply(D, 1, order))
  sapply(ks, function(k) rowMeans(matrix(y_train[ord[, 1:k, drop = FALSE]], nrow(ord))))
}

gen1 <- function(n = 400) {
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), n)
  list(X = X, y = f(X) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.1))
}

x0 <- c(0.5, 0.7, 1)
f0 <- f(matrix(x0, 1))
ks <- seq(1, 29, by = 2)

(a) The true mean response is f(𝒙0)=0.5(0.5)+sin⁡(0.7)−0.3(1)2=0.5942f(\mathbf x_0)=0.5(0.5)+\sin(0.7)-0.3(1)^2=0.5942. Seed: 4325.

one_fit <- knn_reg(d$X, d$y, x0, ks)
knitr::kable(data.frame(k = ks, prediction = round(drop(one_fit), 4)),
             caption = "KNN predictions at x0 from one training dataset.")

The last column confirms MSE=bias2+variance\text{MSE}=\text{bias}^2+\text{variance} up to floating-point error (the largest absolute difference is about 10−1710^{-17}). This is exact, not approximate, because the empirical variance uses divisor 200.

Show the workflow 
matplot(ks, cbind(bias_sq, variance, mse), type = "b", pch = 1:3, lty = 1:3,
        col = 1:3, xlab = "k", ylab = "value", main = "KNN bias-variance at x0")
legend("topright", c("squared bias", "variance", "MSE"), pch = 1:3, lty = 1:3, col = 1:3)

Pattern. At k=1k=1 the prediction is a single noisy response from the nearest point, so variance is large (≈0.037\approx0.037) and bias is almost zero. As kk grows, the prediction averages more responses, so variance falls roughly like σ2/k\sigma^2/k plus the variability in which points are selected. At the same time, the neighborhood reaches farther from 𝒙0\mathbf x_0 into regions where ff is different, so squared bias grows steadily. With three covariates, the neighborhood radius grows quickly with kk. MSE is U-shaped and is smallest near k=9k=9. Past that point, bias dominates.

Comparison with ridge and lasso. The trade-off is the same, but the tuning parameter runs in the same direction as the penalty: larger kk corresponds to larger λ\lambda. Both give a simpler, more stable fit with more bias. The mechanism differs. Ridge and lasso shrink coefficients of a fixed linear model toward zero, and the bias comes from shrinkage (and, for a nonlinear ff, from the linear form itself). KNN makes no global shape assumption; its bias comes from averaging over a wider neighborhood, and its complexity is roughly measured by n/kn/k effective parameters. At λ=0\lambda=0 ridge is OLS, which still has model bias here because ff is nonlinear. KNN at k=1k=1 has almost no bias, so its bias can be driven close to zero in a way that a linear model’s cannot.

Question 2: Compare KNN with lasso

Use the response model from Question 1, including the noise standard deviation 0.10.1, but generate p=30p=30 covariates. The response still depends only on the first three. Consider these two settings:

  • Setting 1: all 30 covariates are independent standard normal variables.

  • Setting 2: the covariates have a multivariate normal distribution with mean zero and covariance matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol\Sigma, where

    Σjj=1,Σjl=0.8for j≠l. \Sigma_{jj}=1, \qquad \Sigma_{jl}=0.8\quad\text{for }j\ne l.

In each setting, generate 400 training observations and 1,000 independent test observations. Fit 5NN using Euclidean distance on the supplied covariate scale. All covariates already have population variance one.

For lasso, use a linear model containing the 30 covariates and a separately fitted, unpenalized intercept. Follow the Week 4 objective,

Lλ(𝜷)=12n∥𝒚̃−𝑿𝜷∥22+λ‖𝜷‖1, L_\lambda(\boldsymbol\beta) =\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert \widetilde{\mathbf y}-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta \right\rVert_2^2 +\lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1,

where 𝑿∈ℝn×30\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times30} contains the centered and standardized covariates and 𝒚̃\widetilde{\mathbf y} is the centered training response. Select the penalty by ten-fold cross-validation over 41 logarithmically spaced values from 10−410^{-4} to 11. Estimate all means and scales using only the training portion of each fold, with divisor equal to that portion’s sample size. After selecting the penalty, refit on all training observations and apply the fitted transformations unchanged to the test observations. Do not add nonlinear terms to the lasso model.

  1. Fit both methods in each setting. Use the same training and test data for the two methods within a setting. Report their test MSE values in one table, together with the selected lasso penalty and the number of nonzero lasso slopes. You only need to generate one dataset for each setting; repeated simulations are not required.

  2. Compare the results between the two settings. Explain how correlation can change the usefulness of Euclidean neighborhoods, and why lasso does not use all covariates in the same way as KNN.

  3. The response model contains sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) and X32X_3^2, but the lasso fit uses only linear terms. Explain how this difference affects the comparison. Would the results justify a general claim that correlation always helps KNN, or that one method is always better? Explain why.

Answer

Setting 2 is generated as 𝑿i=0.8Wi𝟏+0.2𝑼i\mathbf X_i=\sqrt{0.8}\,W_i\mathbf 1+\sqrt{0.2}\,\mathbf U_i with WiW_i and the entries of 𝑼i\mathbf U_i independent standard normal, which gives unit variances and every pairwise covariance 0.80.8. KNN uses knn_reg from Question 1 with k=5k=5.

For lasso, I standardize each fold’s training portion with its own means and scales (divisor equal to that portion’s size), center its response, and fit the whole path with glmnet(standardize = FALSE, intercept = FALSE). For the Gaussian family, glmnet minimizes exactly 12n‖𝒚̃−𝑿𝜷‖22+λ‖𝜷‖1\frac{1}{2n}\lVert\widetilde{\mathbf y}-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2+\lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1. The held-out fold is transformed with the training portion’s means and scales, and its prediction adds back the training-portion mean response.

Show the workflow 
library(glmnet)
Loading required package: Matrix
Loaded glmnet 5.0
Show the workflow 
gen2 <- function(n, rho) {
  U <- matrix(rnorm(n * 30), n)
  X <- if (rho == 0) U else sqrt(rho) * rnorm(n) + sqrt(1 - rho) * U
  list(X = X, y = f(X) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.1))
}

lambda_grid <- 10^seq(-4, 0, length.out = 41)
lambda_dec  <- sort(lambda_grid, decreasing = TRUE)   # glmnet column order

lasso_fit <- function(X, y, lambda) {
  m <- colMeans(X)
  s <- sqrt(colMeans(sweep(X, 2, m)^2))             # divisor = number of rows
  fit <- glmnet(scale(X, m, s), y - mean(y), lambda = sort(lambda, decreasing = TRUE),
                standardize = FALSE, intercept = FALSE)
  list(m = m, s = s, y_bar = mean(y), fit = fit)
}
lasso_predict <- function(obj, X_new) {
  obj$y_bar + as.matrix(scale(X_new, obj$m, obj$s) %*% obj$fit$beta)
}

run_setting <- function(rho, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  tr <- gen2(400, rho); te <- gen2(1000, rho)
  folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = 400))
  cv_err <- sapply(1:10, function(j) {
    obj <- lasso_fit(tr$X[folds != j, ], tr$y[folds != j], lambda_grid)
    colMeans((tr$y[folds == j] - lasso_predict(obj, tr$X[folds == j, , drop = FALSE]))^2)
  })
  lam_hat <- lambda_dec[which.min(rowMeans(cv_err))]
  final <- lasso_fit(tr$X, tr$y, lam_hat)
  beta  <- as.numeric(final$fit$beta)
  list(knn_mse   = mean((te$y - knn_reg(tr$X, tr$y, te$X, 5))^2),
       lasso_mse = mean((te$y - lasso_predict(final, te$X))^2),
       lambda = lam_hat, nonzero = sum(beta != 0), beta = beta,
       var_y = mean((te$y - mean(te$y))^2))
}

s1 <- run_setting(0,   43252)
s2 <- run_setting(0.8, 43253)

(a) Seeds: 43252 (Setting 1) and 43253 (Setting 2).

Show the workflow 
q2_tab <- data.frame(
  setting = c("1: independent", "2: correlation 0.8"),
  knn5_test_MSE  = c(s1$knn_mse, s2$knn_mse),
  lasso_test_MSE = c(s1$lasso_mse, s2$lasso_mse),
  lasso_lambda   = c(s1$lambda, s2$lambda),
  nonzero_slopes = c(s1$nonzero, s2$nonzero),
  test_var_y     = c(s1$var_y, s2$var_y))
knitr::kable(q2_tab, digits = 4)
setting knn5_test_MSE lasso_test_MSE lasso_lambda nonzero_slopes test_var_y
1: independent 0.5681 0.2867 0.0398 5 0.8754
2: correlation 0.8 0.2041 0.3668 0.0200 12 1.3264
Show the workflow 
rbind(setting1 = round(s1$beta[1:3], 3), setting2 = round(s2$beta[1:3], 3))
          [,1]  [,2] [,3]
setting1 0.455 0.578    0
setting2 0.380 0.483    0

(b) The two methods trade places. With independent covariates, lasso’s test MSE (0.2870.287) is about half of 5NN’s (0.5680.568). With correlation 0.80.8, 5NN improves sharply to 0.2040.204 and beats lasso (0.3670.367).

Why correlation helps Euclidean neighborhoods here. KNN measures distance using all 30 coordinates equally, but only the first three affect the response. In Setting 1 the 27 irrelevant coordinates are independent noise. They dominate the squared distance, so the five “nearest” training points are nearest mostly in irrelevant directions and can have very different X1,X2,X3X_1,X_2,X_3. This is the curse of dimensionality: in 30 independent dimensions, 400 points are too sparse to find neighbors that are close in the directions that matter. In Setting 2, most of the variation in each observation comes from one shared factor WiW_i. The points lie near a one-dimensional line with a smaller spread around it, so the data are effectively much lower-dimensional. A point that is close in Euclidean distance also tends to have a similar WiW_i and therefore similar X1,X2,X3X_1,X_2,X_3. The irrelevant coordinates now carry information about the relevant ones instead of pure noise.

Why lasso does not use all covariates equally. Lasso estimates a separate coefficient for each covariate, and the ℓ1\ell_1 penalty sets most of them to exactly zero. In Setting 1 it kept only 55 slopes, with the large ones on X1X_1 and X2X_2, effectively discarding the irrelevant coordinates that damage KNN. KNN has no such mechanism: every coordinate enters the distance with equal weight. In Setting 2, lasso kept 1212 small slopes. Correlation makes the covariates partly interchangeable, so lasso spreads a little weight onto irrelevant covariates that act as proxies for the shared factor.

(c) Lasso can only fit 0.5x1+β2x2+β3x30.5x_1+\beta_2x_2+\beta_3x_3. sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) is roughly linear near zero and lasso captures much of it, but −0.3X32-0.3X_3^2 is an even function with no linear component when X3X_3 is symmetric about zero. So lasso cannot represent it at all, and X3X_3 is dropped in Setting 1. That missing curvature (variance 0.09Var(X32)=0.180.09\,\text{Var}(X_3^2)=0.18) plus the nonlinear part of sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) is a floor that lasso cannot go below, no matter how much data it has. KNN is flexible enough to capture it in principle. The comparison is therefore between a method with high bias but low variance (misspecified lasso) and a method with low bias but high variance in 30 dimensions (KNN). Which wins depends on which error is larger in the specific setting. In Setting 2, correlation also lets lasso leak some of the X32X_3^2 signal into the shared factor, but only as a linear approximation.

These results do not justify either general claim. They come from one dataset per setting and from one specific response function. Correlation helped KNN here because it made the covariates concentrate near a low-dimensional structure that also determines the response. If the response depended on the differences between covariates, such as X1−X2X_1-X_2, those differences have small variance under strong correlation and are swamped by the shared factor in the Euclidean distance, so correlation could hurt KNN. Similarly, if ff were linear, lasso would be close to optimal and would beat KNN in both settings; with a smaller pp or a larger nn, KNN’s variance would shrink and it could win in Setting 1. Neither method is always better. The ranking depends on how well each method’s assumptions match the true structure.

Question 3: Observed dimension and latent dimension

The lecture’s handwritten digit example shows that KNN can work with many measured covariates. We will use a simulation to investigate why the structure of those covariates matters.

Let p=100p=100 be the number of observed covariates and let mm be the number of latent variables. For each observation, generate

𝑿i=𝑨𝒁i+𝜼i,Yi=Zi1+Zi2+ϵi, \mathbf X_i=\mathbf A\mathbf Z_i+\boldsymbol\eta_i, \qquad Y_i=Z_{i1}+Z_{i2}+\epsilon_i,

where 𝑨∈ℝ100×m\mathbf A\in\mathbb R^{100\times m} has independent entries from Uniform[−2,2][-2,2]. The entries of 𝒁i∈ℝm\mathbf Z_i\in\mathbb R^m and 𝜼i∈ℝ100\boldsymbol\eta_i\in\mathbb R^{100}, and the scalar ϵi\epsilon_i, are independent standard normal variables, also independent of 𝑨\mathbf A. Generate 𝑨\mathbf A once and use it for all training and test observations in that dataset.

Compare m=3m=3 and m=30m=30. In each setting, generate 200 training observations and 200 independent test observations. Fit KNN using only the 100 observed covariates in 𝑿\mathbf X, with Euclidean distance on their generated scale. The latent variables in 𝒁\mathbf Z are used to generate the data but are not available to the fitted model. Consider k=2,10,18,…,82k=2,10,18,\ldots,82.

  1. Generate one dataset for each value of mm. Fit KNN for every value of kk and calculate test MSE. Within a setting, use the same training and test observations for all values of kk.

  2. Repeat the complete experiment 50 times, generating a new 𝑨\mathbf A and new observations in each repetition. Plot average test MSE against kk, with one curve for each value of mm. These curves compare the specified choices of kk in a controlled simulation; they are not a cross-validation procedure for selecting a final model.

  3. Both settings have 100 observed covariates, and the response depends on only two latent variables. Explain why their KNN performance can still differ. What role does the noise 𝜼i\boldsymbol\eta_i play, and why are the observed data not confined exactly to an mm-dimensional linear space?

Answer

Show the workflow 
ks3 <- seq(2, 82, by = 8)

# one complete dataset: a new A, then training and test observations sharing it
gen3 <- function(m, n = 200, p = 100) {
  A <- matrix(runif(p * m, -2, 2), p, m)
  draw <- function() {
    Z <- matrix(rnorm(n * m), n, m)
    list(X = Z %*% t(A) + matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p), y = Z[, 1] + Z[, 2] + rnorm(n))
  }
  list(train = draw(), test = draw())
}

knn_test_mse <- function(m) {
  d <- gen3(m)
  colMeans((d$test$y - knn_reg(d$train$X, d$train$y, d$test$X, ks3))^2)
}

(a) Seed: 43254.

Show the workflow

q3a <- rbind(m3 = knn_test_mse(3), m30 = knn_test_mse(30))
colnames(q3a) <- paste0("k=", ks3)

With m=3m=3, the best average test MSE is about 1.271.27 (at k=10k=10), not far above the noise floor of 11 (dotted line). With m=30m=30, it is about 2.32.3, not much below Var(Y)=3\text{Var}(Y)=3, which is what predicting the overall mean would give. Both curves have the usual U shape: very small kk has high variance, and very large kk oversmooths.

(c) KNN performance depends on the dimension of the space in which the data actually vary, not on the number of columns. In both settings 𝑿\mathbf X has 100 columns. With m=3m=3, the signal part 𝑨𝒁i\mathbf A\mathbf Z_i lies in a 3-dimensional subspace of ℝ100\mathbb R^{100}. Distances between observations are then driven by differences in only three latent coordinates, and 200 points are enough to fill a 3-dimensional space densely. Nearby points in 𝑿\mathbf X have nearly the same 𝒁\mathbf Z, and therefore nearly the same Z1+Z2Z_1+Z_2. With m=30m=30, the signal spans 30 dimensions. 200 points are extremely sparse in 30 dimensions, so even the nearest neighbors differ substantially in most latent coordinates, including Z1Z_1 and Z2Z_2. The distance is also dominated by the 28 latent variables that do not affect YY. Since the response depends on only 2 latent variables in both settings, the difference comes entirely from how many irrelevant latent directions dilute the distance.

The noise 𝜼i\boldsymbol\eta_i adds an independent standard normal perturbation to every one of the 100 coordinates. Because it is full-rank, the observed 𝑿i\mathbf X_i are not confined to the mm-dimensional column space of 𝑨\mathbf A. They lie in a thin cloud around it with spread in all 100 directions. 𝜼i\boldsymbol\eta_i adds to every squared distance a random term with mean 2×100=2002\times100=200, which is unrelated to YY and blurs the neighbor ranking. KNN still works when m=3m=3 because the signal is much stronger than this noise. Each column of 𝑨\mathbf A has squared length about 100×43≈133100\times\frac{4}{3}\approx133, so a unit change in one latent variable moves 𝑿\mathbf X much farther than the noise in a typical direction. The latent structure therefore dominates the distances. This is the same reason KNN works on handwritten digits: the 256 pixels are strongly dependent and lie near a low-dimensional set of plausible digit shapes, plus small pixel-level noise.

Question 4: Classify handwritten digits

Use zip.train and zip.test from the R package ElemStatLearn, as in the lecture. The package has been retired from the active CRAN repository. If needed, install the archived package into your usual R library, then load the two datasets. Python users can use the course copies of the same training data and test data. These compressed CSV files have no headers and are included in the homework ZIP under data/knn. Run the Python code from the folder containing data.

Each image has 16×16=25616\times16=256 pixel values. The first column is the digit label and the remaining columns are the pixel values. Use the first 1,000 rows of zip.train and the first 500 rows of zip.test. Use the original pixel values without standardization, and do not include the digit label in a distance calculation.

For a test image 𝒙0\mathbf x_0 and a training image 𝒙i\mathbf x_i, the two distances are

dE(𝒙0,𝒙i)=∑j=1256(x0j−xij)2,dM(𝒙0,𝒙i)=∑j=1256|x0j−xij|. d_E(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf x_i) =\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{256}(x_{0j}-x_{ij})^2}, \qquad d_M(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf x_i) =\sum_{j=1}^{256}|x_{0j}-x_{ij}|.

  1. Write a 5NN classification function that allows either Euclidean or Manhattan distance. For each test image, calculate its distances to the training images directly, find the five nearest, and return the most frequent digit label. Break distance ties by the smaller training row number and voting ties by the smallest digit. Do not use a built-in distance or KNN function for this part.

  2. Apply the classifier to all 500 test images using each distance. For each fit, report the test classification error and a 10×1010\times10 confusion matrix, with rows representing predicted digits and columns representing true digits. Keep all digit labels from 0 through 9 in the matrix, including any with a zero count. Which digits are most often confused with one another?

  3. For Euclidean distance, display three incorrectly classified test images, together with their true and predicted labels. Comment on whether the mistakes are visually understandable. Compare the overall results of the two distance measures. Can they have similar total error while making mistakes on different images? Use your predictions to support your answer.

Answer

Show the workflow 
library(ElemStatLearn)
train <- zip.train[1:1000, ]
test  <- zip.test[1:500, ]
X_train <- train[, -1]; label_train <- train[, 1]
X_test  <- test[, -1];  label_test  <- test[, 1]

(a) For each test image, the function computes the absolute pixel differences to all training images and forms either the Euclidean or the Manhattan distance by hand. It then takes the five smallest. order() is stable, so equal distances keep the smaller training row number first. The votes are counted for digits 0 to 9, and which.max() returns the first maximum, which is the smallest tied digit.

Show the workflow 
knn5_classify <- function(X_train, label_train, X_test, distance = c("euclidean", "manhattan")) {
  distance <- match.arg(distance)
  apply(X_test, 1, function(x0) {
    diffs <- abs(sweep(X_train, 2, x0))
    d <- if (distance == "euclidean") sqrt(rowSums(diffs^2)) else rowSums(diffs)
    nearest <- order(d)[1:5]                        # ties -> smaller row number
    votes <- tabulate(label_train[nearest] + 1, nbins = 10)
    which.max(votes) - 1                            # ties -> smallest digit
  })
}

# most frequent confusions, combining both directions of each pair
top_pairs <- function(conf) {
  off <- conf + t(conf); off[lower.tri(off, diag = TRUE)] <- 0
  idx <- order(off, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]
  data.frame(pair = paste(row(off)[idx] - 1, col(off)[idx] - 1, sep = " & "), count = off[idx])
}
knitr::kable(cbind(top_pairs(conf_E), top_pairs(conf_M)),
             col.names = c("Euclidean pair", "count", "Manhattan pair", "count"))
Euclidean pair count Manhattan pair count
0 & 2 7 0 & 2 6
3 & 5 5 7 & 9 6
4 & 9 5 0 & 5 5
7 & 9 5 3 & 5 5
0 & 5 4 4 & 9 5

The test error is 12.2% for Euclidean distance and 13.8% for Manhattan distance. For both distances, the most common confusion is a true 2 predicted as 0, followed by 0 and 5, 3 and 5, 4 and 9, and 7 and 9. These pairs share most of their strokes: a 4 with a nearly closed top looks like a 9, and a 7 with a curled top looks like a 9. A 3 and a 5 share the same lower curve, and a loosely written 2 or 5 can form a loop like a 0. Zero is also by far the most common digit in the 1,000 training images (213 of them), so it wins many close votes.

(c)

Show the workflow 
wrong_E <- which(pred_E != label_test)
# one example each of three frequent confusions (true -> predicted)
show <- sapply(list(c(4, 9), c(5, 3), c(2, 0)), function(tp)
  wrong_E[label_test[wrong_E] == tp[1] & pred_E[wrong_E] == tp[2]][1])

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2.5, 0.5))
for (i in show) {
  img <- matrix(X_test[i, ], 16, 16, byrow = TRUE)
  image(t(img[16:1, ]), col = gray(seq(1, 0, length.out = 256)), axes = FALSE, asp = 1,
        main = sprintf("test row %d: true %d, predicted %d", i, label_test[i], pred_E[i]))
}

The mistakes are visually understandable. Each image is an unusual or sloppy version of its true digit that lies closer, pixel by pixel, to typical images of the predicted digit: a 4 whose two upper arms curve toward each other like the loop of a 9, a very thick 5 whose top bar is barely visible so that mostly the curved body it shares with a 3 remains, and a 2 whose top curve and long bottom stroke nearly close into a loop like a 0. Pixel distance has no idea of stroke order or small gaps, which a person uses to tell these digits apart.

Show the workflow 
wrong_M <- pred_M != label_test
table(euclidean = ifelse(pred_E != label_test, "wrong", "right"),
      manhattan = ifelse(wrong_M, "wrong", "right"))
         manhattan
euclidean right wrong
    right   428    11
    wrong     3    58

The two distances give similar overall results: 61 versus 69 errors out of 500, with nearly identical confusion matrices. They do not make exactly the same mistakes, though. 58 images are misclassified by both, 3 only by Euclidean distance, and 11 only by Manhattan distance. So two classifiers can have similar total error while disagreeing on individual images. Squaring differences makes Euclidean distance emphasize a few large pixel mismatches, such as a stroke in a different place. Manhattan distance weights many small mismatches more, which changes the neighbor set for borderline images. Most errors are shared, however, because both distances use the same raw pixels. The hard images, like those shown above, are genuinely closer to the wrong class under either metric.

Create a short SKILL.md file for improving the formatting of STAT 432 homework plots. You may use AI to help write it.

Your rules should address margins, titles, axes, labels, colors, and sizes for plots produced in R or Python. Keep them portable: do not refer to specific homework questions.

  2. Ask your agent to install the skill. Explicitly call it to improve the plot from Question 1, then compare the original and revised versions. Do you like the changes? You may revise the skill and test it a couple more times, or uninstall it if it remains unhelpful.

  3. Append your final SKILL.md content to your submission and briefly explain your choices and experience.

Answer

(a) I wrote the skill with the help of my AI agent (Claude Code) and saved it as plot-formatting/SKILL.md. Its description limits it to improving STAT 432 homework plots and says it may be used only when I explicitly ask for it. The rules cover margins, titles, axes, labels, colors, and sizes, in wording that applies to both base R/ggplot2 and matplotlib, and they never mention a particular question.

(b) The agent installed the skill with Claude Code’s normal method, by copying the folder into the personal skills directory ~/.claude/skills/plot-formatting/. I then explicitly asked it to use plot-formatting to improve the Question 1 bias-variance plot. It first stated what the plot shows (three error components against kk from 200 repetitions), then returned the code below with this list of changes:

  • Margins: set par(mar = ...) so the labels fit without the wide default top margin.
  • Title: shortened to “Bias-variance trade-off for KNN at x0”; moved “200 repetitions, n = 400” to a subtitle.
  • Axes: y-axis starts at 0; x-axis ticks placed at the odd values of kk actually used.
  • Labels: “k” became “Number of neighbors, k”; “value” became “Error at x0”.
  • Colors: replaced default black/red/green with Okabe-Ito blue, orange, and bluish green; kept distinct line types and point shapes.
  • Sizes: line width 2, slightly larger points, legend without a box so it does not hide data.
  • No gridlines or other decoration added.
Show the workflow 
okabe_ito <- c("#0072B2", "#E69F00", "#009E73")
op <- par(mar = c(4.2, 4.5, 3.2, 1))
matplot(ks, cbind(bias_sq, variance, mse), type = "b", pch = c(16, 17, 15), lty = c(1, 2, 1),
        lwd = 2, cex = 1.1, col = okabe_ito, ylim = c(0, max(mse, variance) * 1.05), xaxt = "n",
        xlab = "Number of neighbors, k", ylab = "Error at x0",
        main = "Bias-variance trade-off for KNN at x0", cex.lab = 1.1)
axis(1, at = ks)
mtext("200 repetitions, n = 400 training observations each", side = 3, line = 0.3, cex = 0.9)
legend("topright", c("Squared bias", "Variance", "Mean squared error"), col = okabe_ito,
       pch = c(16, 17, 15), lty = c(1, 2, 1), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
Show the workflow 
par(op)

Comparison. The original plot (in Question 1) was correct, but it used R’s default black, red, and green, which are hard to tell apart for red-green colorblind readers. Its axis labels were the uninformative “k” and “value”, and the x-axis did not show which kk were used. The revised version is clearly easier to read: the axis labels say what is plotted, the ticks match the fitted values of kk, the y-axis starting at 0 makes the relative sizes of bias and variance honest, and the thicker, colorblind-safe lines are distinguishable even in grayscale. I liked the changes. Importantly, the skill changed only formatting; the data and plot type are the same. It did not need revising, so I kept it installed.

(c) My choices: I kept the description narrow and required an explicit request so the skill never fires on its own during ordinary work, which is what made the Week 3 skill easy to live with. I phrased every rule as a principle (“label every axis with the quantity in words”) rather than library-specific code, so it works in R or Python and on any future homework. I asked the agent to list its changes in one line each, which made it easy to check that it had not changed the analysis. The complete skill is appended below under plot-formatting skill.

plot-formatting skill

---
name: plot-formatting
description: Improve the formatting of an existing STAT 432 homework plot in R or Python. Use only when the student explicitly asks to use plot-formatting on a specific plot; never apply it on your own.
---

# plot-formatting

**Intent:** I want homework plots that a grader can read at a glance. Improve how a plot looks without changing what it shows.

## Instructions

1. Read the plotting code and identify what the plot is meant to show.
2. Apply the rules below, changing formatting only. Keep the same data, computed values, and plot type.
3. Show the revised code and list each change in one short line.

## Rules

- **Margins:** trim wasted outer space, but leave enough room that axis labels, tick labels, and the legend are never clipped.
- **Title:** one short line stating what is plotted. Put setup details (sample size, number of repetitions) in a subtitle or caption, not the title.
- **Axes:** start each axis where the data make sense; use a log scale only if values span several orders of magnitude. Put tick marks at meaningful values, such as the values actually used for a tuning parameter.
- **Labels:** label every axis with the quantity in words, plus its symbol or units (for example, "Number of neighbors, k"). Never leave a raw variable name as a label. Prefer labeling lines directly or placing the legend inside an empty region of the plot.
- **Colors:** use at most one color per series, from a colorblind-safe palette (Okabe-Ito in R or Python). Also distinguish series by line type or point shape so the plot still works in grayscale.
- **Sizes:** text should be readable at the rendered size (about 11-12 pt); lines at least 1.5 pt wide; points visible but not overlapping the lines they mark. Set figure width and height explicitly, typically about 7 by 4.5 inches.
- Do not add decorations that carry no information (3-D effects, heavy grids, background colors, shadows).
